source: Species chosen from the Invasive Species Centre and the Invading Species Awareness Program profiles. iNaturalist taxon ids looked up live on 2026-09-19 via GET https://api.inaturalist.org/v1/taxa?q=<name>&rank=species.

tell: Invasive stands are extremely dense, up to 200 stems per square metre; native stands are usually not as dense.
Invasive stems are tan or beige with blue-green leaves; native stems are more reddish-brown with yellow-green leaves.
Invasive seedheads are large and dense; native seedheads are smaller and sparser.
Invasive plants reach up to 5 metres.

guide.compares: cow parsnip, giant hogweed, Queen Anne's lace, angelica
tell: Wild parsnip: up to 1.5 m, a single smooth green stem 2 to 5 cm thick, yellowish-green flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters 10 to 20 cm across, leaflets sharply toothed and shaped like a mitten.
Cow parsnip (native): taller, 1 to 2.5 m, white flowers in clusters 10 to 30 cm across, leaves lobed like a hand with fuzzy undersides.
Giant hogweed: 2.5 to 5 m, hollow stems with purple blotches and coarse bristly hairs, white flower clusters 30 to 90 cm across.
Queen Anne's lace: 0.3 to 1.5 m, white flower cluster 5 to 10 cm across, finely divided feathery leaves.
Angelica (native): 1.2 to 2.1 m, greenish-white globe-like flower clusters, smooth purple or purple-blotched stem.

guide.compares: milkweed (the source describes dog-strangling vine but gives no direct comparison)
tell: A vine that grows 1 to 2 m high by twining onto plants, trees or structures.
Leaves oval with a pointed tip, 7 to 12 cm long, on opposite sides of the stem.
Pink to dark purple star-shaped flowers with five petals 5 to 9 mm long.
Bean-shaped seed pods 4 to 7 cm long that release feathery white seeds in late summer.

guide.compares: cow parsnip, angelica, Queen Anne's lace
tell: Giant hogweed grows up to 5.5 m; the lookalikes are not as large as a mature plant.
Thick hollow stems with reddish-purple flecks and stiff hairs filled with sap.
White flower clusters more widely spaced than Queen Anne's lace, forming a head almost one metre wide.

guide.compares: fireweed, blue vervain, blazing stars, native winged and swamp loosestrife (the source names them but gives no direct comparison)
tell: Stems are woody and square; one rhizome can produce 30 to 50 erect stems up to 2.4 m high.
Leaves opposite or whorled, 3 to 10 cm long, with smooth edges.
Flowers with five to seven pink-purple petals about 10 mm long on long spikes at the top of the stems; in flower June to early August.
Crushed leaves and twigs give off a foul smell ("stinky sumac").
Leaflets have smooth margins except for one or two lobes near the base; native sumac leaflets are toothed.
Smooth, pale grey bark; clusters of small yellowish-green flowers that become winged samaras.
Asian long-horned beetle: shiny black with prominent, irregular white spots, distinct bluish-white legs, black and white banded antennae, 2 to 4 cm.
Whitespotted sawyer (native): black with one distinct white spot behind the head, strong reddish legs, plain black antennae, 1 to 3 cm, generally on conifers.
